title: Same Spelling, New Sense
objectives: I can tell which meaning a word has by reading the sentence around it.
I can say a word two ways when the meaning and the stress change, like record and present.
I can use the roots duct and ject to understand words like conduct and object.
I can write two sentences that show two meanings of the same word.
rationale: Many of the most common words students meet in science and math have more than one meaning, and several change their stress and sound with the meaning (record, present, object, produce, content, conduct). Students who know only the everyday meaning stumble on volume in math, degree in science, and figure in a graph. The unit puts ten such words in one place, gives each a main sense and one or two other senses, and uses a science-fair passage so that students must read for context. Two roots (duct, lead; ject, throw) add a small word-study strand and link back to unit 3.

passage.title: Rosa's Plant Project
paras: Rosa and her partner Omar decided to conduct an experiment for the science fair. They wanted to learn how much light helps plants grow. Each day, they would record the height of three bean plants.

First, they measured the volume of water for each pot, exactly one cup a day. One plant sat in a dark closet, one by a window, and one under a lamp. The room stayed at seventy degrees, so temperature could not change the results.

After three weeks, the plant by the window had produced the most leaves. When Omar looked at the figures in their chart, he could hardly believe the difference. The plant in the closet had barely grown at all.

On fair day, Rosa and Omar stood beside their poster to present their findings. The content was simple: a chart, a photograph, and a short summary. One judge started to object to the small size of the sample, but Rosa explained that they had repeated the test twice. The judge nodded and wrote down a score.
That night, Rosa felt content. Next spring, she hopes to plant a garden to see how much food it will yield.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, what does the word "conduct" mean?
qs.why: They decided to carry out an experiment, so conduct means to carry out.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, which meaning of "present" is used?
choices: To show and explain to others
qs.why: Rosa and Omar stood beside their poster to share their findings with the judges.

qs.q: Why did Rosa and Omar keep the room at the same temperature?
choices: Because the judges asked them to
So the plants would get colder
So the room would be quiet
So only the amount of light would be different between the plants
qs.why: If the temperature stayed the same, only light could explain the difference in growth.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that light helped the plants grow?
choices: The room stayed at seventy degrees.
The plant by the window produced the most leaves, and the closet plant barely grew.
qs.why: The growth of each plant compared with the light it got is the evidence.

qs.q: What is the passage mostly about?
choices: Two students who planned, tested, and shared an experiment about plants
qs.why: The passage follows Rosa and Omar through their whole experiment.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that mean more than one thing. Six are heteronyms whose stress or sound changes with the meaning. The science-fair passage uses almost every word, and the study task has students say a word two ways and name each meaning.

notes.va.figure.n: Start with the sentence frame: a figure in a graph, a figure in a story. Students often know only the shape sense. Show both on the board.
notes.va.volume.n: Three senses: space, loudness, and a book. Ask students to hold up three fingers and show which sense a sentence uses. Link to math volume of a box.
notes.va.degree.n: Temperature and angle share the symbol. Ask which tool (thermometer or protractor) goes with each. The senses of level and college title are shown but are not required.
notes.va.yield.v: Link to the road sign: a yield sign. The crop sense is a second use; a field yields a harvest. Ask students which sense a sentence uses.
notes.va.produce.v: Teach the verb pruh-DOOS and mention the noun PROH-doos (fruits and vegetables). The word comes from a Latin word meaning to lead forth, the same lead root found in conduct and product.
notes.va.record.v: Verb: rih-KORD. Noun: REK-erd. Clap the stress pattern. Students often use only the noun; have them say both and write a sentence for each.
notes.va.present.v: Verb: prih-ZENT. Noun and adjective: PREZ-ent. Use a gift box and a poster to show the two. Ask students for a sentence in which the sound is clear from the meaning.
notes.va.object.v: Verb: ub-JEKT. Noun: OB-jekt. The ject root means throw; to object is to throw words against an idea. Connect to reject and project from unit 3.
notes.va.content.n: Noun: KON-tent. Adjective: kun-TENT. Both meanings are taught here, with the noun as the main sense. Compare the contents of a box with feeling content.
notes.va.conduct.v: Verb: kun-DUKT. Noun: KON-dukt (behavior). Show duct as lead: a conductor leads. Students often confuse conduct with the word control.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The sentence says, "We will ___ the choir." I see the word choir, so I think of a person leading singers. Conduct, said kun-DUKT, means to lead. If I see the same word in "good ___," I read it KON-dukt, behavior. The meaning tells me how to say it.'
discuss: Which words in this unit change how they sound when the meaning changes?
How can you tell which meaning an author wants?
misconceptions: Heteronyms are spelled differently when they sound different.
extend: Make a two-column chart of word, meaning 1, meaning 2 for six words from your reading.
Write a short poem that uses a heteronym twice, once for each meaning.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Return to the heteronyms two days later with a say-it-two-ways drill. At one week, use volume, degree, and figure in a math journal entry.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (cifra, volumen, grado, ceder, producir, registrar; grabar, presentar, objetar, contenido, realizar; dirigir) not reviewed by a native speaker; check sense match for each word.

Respelling of the noun/verb pairs (pruh-DOOS vs PROH-doos; rih-KORD vs REK-erd; prih-ZENT vs PREZ-ent; ub-JEKT vs OB-jekt; KON-tent vs kun-TENT; kun-DUKT vs KON-dukt) is correct for US English; confirm for classroom use.
Etymology claims are limited to Latin lead (duct) and throw (ject) roots; confirm the note that produce comes from a Latin word meaning to lead forth.
